title: Search In Rotated Sorted Array
statement: A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated at some unknown spot, so it is a high run followed by a low run. Given the rotated array and a target, return the target's index, or -1 if it is missing. Aim for O(log n).

example.caption: The array is not sorted overall, but it is made of two sorted runs. Target 0 sits in the low run at index 4.

idea.sentence: After you pick the middle, one side of it is always in order. Check if the target fits in that ordered side, and keep it or drop it.

jargon.plain: A sorted array cut at one spot with the two pieces swapped. You get a high run, then a low run.
The part of l..r on one side of m whose values simply increase. You can test a target against its two ends.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: a rotated sorted array and a target, e.g. [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] and 0

compare.optimalLabel: Keep the half that can hold it

rows.name: Linear scan
rows.note: Always works, but ignores the sorted runs.

rows.name: One-pass binary search
rows.note: Each step finds an ordered side, tests the target against its ends, and drops one half.

fast.takeaway: Rotation breaks global order, but not local order. One half is always sorted, and a sorted half can answer a range question.

stages.title: Live range
stages.note: l and r bound the part that could still hold the target.

stages.title: Look at the middle
stages.note: While the range is not empty, take the middle m, rounded down.

stages.title: Find the ordered side
stages.note: nums[l] <= nums[m] means the left side is in order. Otherwise the right side is.

stages.title: Keep or drop
stages.note: If the target fits between the ends of the ordered side, go that way. If not, go the other way.

stages.title: Answer
stages.note: If nums[m] is the target, return m. If l passes r, nothing is left: return -1.

edges.title: Not rotated
edges.why: The left side is always in order, so it behaves like a plain binary search.

edges.title: Single element
edges.why: l = r = 0, the middle is not the target, and one drop empties the range.

edges.title: Two elements, middle is l
edges.why: m = 0 = l, so nums[l] <= nums[m] is true: the left side (just m) is 'ordered'. The target is not in it, so go right. Using <= makes this work.

edges.title: Target in the far low run
edges.why: The middle 8 has an ordered left side 6..8 that cannot hold 2, so the search jumps into the low run.

gotchas.text: Use nums[l] <= nums[m], not <. When l equals m (two cells left) they are the same cell, and with < you would call the right side ordered when it is not.
The range checks need one strict and one loose end: nums[l] <= target && target < nums[m]. nums[m] was already ruled out, so it must not count as inside.
Test the target against the ordered side only. The unordered side contains the drop, and a range check on its ends tells you nothing.
Check nums[m] == target first, before choosing a side, so the middle is never confused with an end of its own range.

recap.pattern: Binary search on a rotated array
recap.key: One side of the middle is always sorted. If the target fits inside that side keep it, otherwise keep the other side.
moves: l = 0, r = n - 1. Take m and return it if it matches
nums[l] <= nums[m]: left is ordered. Else right is ordered
Target inside the ordered side: go there. Else go the other way
